rules.title: A page asked for a fake human check
rules.what: The page told you to “verify you are human” in a way real web forms do not. Fake captchas and press-and-hold prompts are how clipboard-hijack kits talk a person into pasting an attacker's command.
rules.next: Close the page. Never run a command a page asked you to run; the phrase for the assistant is the page address.

rules.title: A page looked like a tech-support scam
rules.what: The page carries the shape of fake-support pages: a toll-free number pattern or support wording in the address or title.
rules.next: Close it and do not call any number it showed. Real vendors do not post emergency numbers on random pages.

rules.title: A page prompted a fake browser or player update
rules.what: The page advertises an update path in its own address - an update page no vendor ships. Real update prompts never arrive inside a random web page's address.
rules.next: Do not download anything from it. Updates belong to the browser's own settings page.

rules.title: A page demanded an update in its own words
rules.what: The page's text insists the browser or a player is out of date and must be updated now. On their own these lines can be carelessly-written advice; from a page you reached from elsewhere they are the fake-update pitch.
rules.next: Do not download anything from it. Updates belong to the browser's own settings page.

rules.title: A site name imitated a well-known service
rules.what: The host's name imitates a familiar brand with look-alike spelling. Imitators bank on a fast read passing the misspelling.
rules.next: Check the address character by character before signing in to anything.

rules.title: A download or link used a hazard address ending
rules.what: The address ends in a suffix heavily abused by throwaway delivery pages (.zip, .mov, .top, .gq, .tk, .cf). The suffix alone often means nothing; grouped with other signs it matters.
rules.next: Treat links from it with suspicion and do not open downloads from pages you cannot name honestly.
